cells.tense: Right now your hands are on what you chose to carry, and you know it
cells.ask: Say one sentence today to the person who should hear it — 'this is what's on my hands' — and leave the room with one other person knowing what you're carrying.
cells.core:
You know what you're carrying and why, and it doesn't have to look heavy to count. Meals happen, bills get paid, the thing keeps going because you keep it going. Nothing dramatic — just a steadiness that shows up daily without needing an audience. That steadiness is also what keeps the weight unwitnessed, and what's on you right now is real and still going.

Saying one line to one person doesn't put anything down; it just lets one load be known where it belongs. What someone hands back is usually smaller than the dread of asking — a nod, a short answer, a look that says they see it.

cells.tense: You're leaning into what's next, staying ahead of a future you can't write in yet
cells.ask: Take the one thing you're already carrying and stop short of finishing it today — leave the last piece undone on purpose, somewhere you'll see it.
cells.core:
You see ahead. Your hand is already out to stop what could go wrong, and that foresight has kept you from being caught out — it's a real skill. Right now it's also running you: loads held that nobody handed you, tomorrow's weight spent on today's strength. The strength you spend bracing is strength that isn't there for what's actually in front of you.

Vision works better coming out of what you've already lived than out of what you fear ahead. Stopping one thing short, on purpose and visibly, hands back the room to see what's here today. The unfinished piece isn't failure — it's proof you don't have to carry everything before it arrives.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already shut, watching the piles from the doorway
cells.ask: Pick the smallest unfinished thing you can see — one dish, one pile, one call — and finish just that piece today, then leave it where you can see it's done.
cells.core:
You know what needs holding. It's right there. What's gone quiet is the moment where the load becomes yours to carry through — the move from seeing it to picking it up. So things sit. Not because they're heavy, but because the strength that would take them on isn't on duty right now. That's not the same as gone.

Watching a finished thing stay finished is what refills the tank. One piece done and seen holding is how the picking-up comes back. Trying harder to bear more doesn't do it — the body learns trust from small completed acts, not from pressure. What comes is a sense that the next thing won't be what breaks you.

cells.tense: Your hands are already on it — the keeping runs while you call it something else
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been filing under the household's or the job's account and say out loud to one person, 'this is mine' — just the naming, nothing changes about the work.
cells.core:
You're already keeping things going. Meals, bills, the small repairs that stop things falling — they happen because of how you show up and what you notice. Ask about it and something else answers: just getting through, it's what has to be done, it isn't really yours. The work is real. The name on it is missing.

When this runs cleanly, the keeping isn't happening around you — it's held by your hands, and it shows in how you move through a room, how the place looks when you leave. Saying 'mine' about one piece doesn't add weight; it puts the person doing the work on the record, and hands back a steadier sense of where it comes from.

attempts.check: What's claimed beyond the record: that a person in Fortitude lets care slip through without picking it up, or drives so hard they can't stop. The record supplies the capacity, not the behavior. A reader could say 'I still do everything, I just do it quietly' — the exit is that the reading points to a place to look, not a verdict. The asks survive being wrong: each one gives back a piece of information about the person's own handling, whether or not the pattern fits. The line serving the writer more than the reader would be any saying that holding so much means you give in silence; that performing the weight as proof of care is what's dropped — the tense is kept in plain words about where the person stands in time.
